common_name: Rancho White Agapanthus (Dwarf White Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Rancho White is a dwarf sport closely related to 'Peter Pan' but bearing pure white flowers, and is sometimes sold under the trade name 'Peter Pan Albus'.

directions: Set out divisions in spring in rich, well-drained soil, spacing plants roughly a foot apart for a dense low edging or container planting. Rancho White forms a compact, narrow-leaved clump topped in summer by rounded umbels of pure white, bell-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, flowering reliably even when slightly pot-bound. It tolerates somewhat cooler conditions than many evergreen Agapanthus, remaining semi-evergreen rather than fully deciduous in borderline winters, and benefits from mulch where temperatures dip below 20F. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the clump and divide only when flowering noticeably declines.

common_name: Isis Agapanthus (Deep Blue Border Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Isis is an RHS-listed deciduous border selection valued for unusually deep, saturated blue flower color.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist but well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing clumps 18-24 inches apart to allow the broad strap-shaped leaves room to spread. Isis produces dense, rounded umbels of narrowly tubular, deep blue flowers on sturdy erect stems through summer, set off by dark grey-green foliage that dies back in autumn. It is hardier than many evergreen Agapanthus thanks to its deciduous habit, and performs well in large containers that can be moved under cover in regions with cold, wet winters. Deadhead after flowering and mulch the crown for winter protection in marginal zones.

common_name: Blue Yonder Agapanthus (Cold-Hardy Repeat-Flowering Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Yonder is among the more cold-hardy Agapanthus selections in cultivation, bred by Oregon plantsman Steve Hottovy and grown by specialist nurseries for its unusually long repeat-flowering season.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing clumps 18-24 inches apart to give the strap-like foliage room to fill in. Blue Yonder sends up sturdy 3-foot stalks topped with dense, rounded clusters of deep cobalt-blue, nectar-rich flowers from late spring and continues flowering intermittently into fall on established plants, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies. Its deciduous habit and improved root hardiness let it survive winters well beyond the range of typical evergreen Agapanthus, though a thick mulch over the crown is still wise at the colder end of its range. Divide congested clumps every several years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Princess Claire Alstroemeria (White Peruvian Lily with Yellow Flash)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Claire ('Zapriclair') is a compact white-flowered member of the Princess Lily series bred by Royal Van Zanten in the Netherlands.

directions: Set out tuberous roots in spring, laying the brittle fingers shallowly rather than burying them deep, since Princess Lily types root more fibrously than full-size garden Alstroemeria. Princess Claire bears crisp white flowers with a faint yellow splotch and fine maroon streaking on a naturally low, tidy mound suited to patio pots and border edges. Pull spent flowering stems from the base rather than cutting them to encourage continuous rebloom through the season, and protect containers from hard freezes since dwarf Princess types are less cold-tolerant in pots than in open ground.

common_name: Princess Paola Alstroemeria (Pink and Yellow Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Paola ('Stapripal') is a compact Princess Lily series selection bred by Royal Van Zanten in the Netherlands.

directions: Set out tuberous roots in spring, spreading the brittle fingers shallowly in loose, well-drained soil in full sun. Princess Paola forms a dense, clump-forming mound to about a foot tall, bearing funnel-shaped flowers in pale to dark pink and yellow streaked with magenta from early summer into fall. Deadhead by pulling whole spent stems from the base to trigger continuous rebloom rather than snipping at the flower, and mulch the crown heavily over winter where marginally hardy, since potted dwarf Princess types are more cold-sensitive than garden-grown full-size Alstroemeria.

common_name: Princess Tamara Alstroemeria (Deep Purple-Pink Dwarf Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Princess Tamara is a dwarf, long-flowering Princess Lily series selection.

directions: Plant tuberous roots in spring, laying the brittle fingers shallowly in loose, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants about a foot apart for container or border-edge display. Princess Tamara produces deep purple-pink flowers with a small yellow flash on the upper petals, held on a compact, tidy mound that blooms over a long season from summer into fall. Pull spent stems from the base to encourage rebloom, and protect containers from hard freezes since this dwarf patio type is less winter-hardy than full-size garden Alstroemeria.

common_name: Archiduc Charles Rose (Color-Changing Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Archiduc Charles is an early-19th-century French China rose, commonly attributed to the breeder/introducer Laffay, grown for flowers that darken dramatically with heat and sun exposure.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Archiduc Charles opens pale pink to carmine but deepens toward dark crimson-purple as each bloom ages and as the weather grows hotter, often showing several shades of pink and red on the same bush at once, flowering in repeated flushes from spring through frost. It is a reliable, twiggy grower with good heat and humidity tolerance typical of the China class. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood, since heavy cutting sacrifices the small twiggy growth that carries most of its bloom.

common_name: Mrs. Bosanquet Rose (Blush Pink China-Bourbon Found Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Mrs. Bosanquet is an 1832 Laffay rose of mixed China and Bourbon heritage, bearing flat, quartered blooms reminiscent of Souvenir de la Malmaison in miniature.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2.5-3.5 feet apart. Mrs. Bosanquet bears clusters of small, flat, quartered double flowers in a delicate blush pink that deepens toward the center, carried on wiry, typically China-type canes, with repeated flushes from spring through frost. Its mixed China-Bourbon ancestry gives it good heat tolerance plus fuller flower form than most pure China roses. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and maintain an open, airy habit.

common_name: Crimson Giant Raspberry (Large-Fruited Late-Season Fall Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring as soon as ground can be worked; Crimson Giant was released by Cornell University's berry breeding program at Geneva, NY, bred by Courtney Weber from a cross of 'Titan' x NY950.

directions: Plant dormant canes in early spring in full sun and fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil, spacing canes 2-3 feet apart in rows. Crimson Giant is a primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry noted for unusually large, firm, bright red fruit and a late ripening window that extends the fresh raspberry harvest into late fall, well past earlier-ripening varieties. Manage it as a primocane type by mowing or cutting all canes to the ground in late winter for a single large autumn crop, and provide consistent irrigation through fruit development to support its oversized berries.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
